description: We are a team of students from Chile passionate about technology, programming, and design. Combining our diverse skills with creativity and innovation, we strive to develop meaningful solutions and explore new possibilities through technology. Above all, we believe that great ideas come from thinking outside the box and working together.
summary:
BeeYond-Mars is an interactive space mission design game and simulation focused on transporting bumblebees colonies to Mars. We developed a mission-planning experience that integrates real interplanetary trajectories using NASA’s Trajectory Browser and General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT) alongside biological diapause protocols.

Our project directly addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by turning complex orbital mechanics, delta-v constraints, and life-support trade-offs into accessible, strategic gameplay. Players must balance launch windows, fuel budgets, and hibernation parameters to ensure colony survival during transit.

This matters because sustainable human settlements on Mars will require closed-loop agricultural ecosystems, where pollinators play a critical role. By gamifying real astrodynamics and biological engineering, BeeYond-Mars inspires students and future mission designers to solve authentic multi-disciplinary spaceflight problems.
details:
What It Does & How It Works:

BeeYond Mars is a browser-based, bilingual (English/Spanish) 8-bit space mission design and simulation game for 1–4 players. Playing as researcher Lum—who finally secures a high-risk 2,000-credit grant from Aurelia Funds after 41 rejected proposals—players assemble an interdisciplinary team and engineer a spacecraft to transport fertilized bumblebee queens (Bombus terrestris) in diapause inside an automated life-support chamber (2.5 °C, 70% RH) to a sealed Martian greenhouse.

The experience unfolds across four connected phases:

1. Story & Team Assembly: Players explore "The Garden of Orbits" (an 8-room, 480×270 pixel-art town) and complete cooperative tasks to recruit Pip (Engineering), Nim (Biology), and Eko (Communications).

2. Spacecraft Engineering & Trade-Off Lab: Using a shared budget, players compare three launcher/bus packages (Scout, Aurelia, Atlaswing) and configure eight subsystems (including Economy vs. Vanguard Active-Control Chambers, Extra Solar Panels, Redundant Thermal Sensor, Repair Toolkit, High-Gain Antenna, Backup Comms, and Radiation Dosimeter) while passing JPL-inspired Concept Maturity Level reviews (CML 1–4) that unlock additional funding.

3. Interplanetary Transit Simulation: Players choose between two real 2030–2031 Earth–Mars trajectories from NASA Ames Trajectory Browser (288-day Standard or 272-day Fast transfer). During the 30-day-stepped voyage, daily GMAT-propagated heliocentric data drives solar irradiance drop-off (1/r²) and one-way signal latency, while seeded thermal alarms, solar storms, and micrometeorite impacts require autonomous onboard decisions under configurable timers.

4. Explainable Mission Paper & Redesign Loop: Post-flight, the game generates a 100-point peer-reviewed mission report (Equipment, In-Flight Decisions, Reserves) explaining exact engineering and biological root causes, allowing players to redesign using the same scenario seed.

Benefits & Intended Impact:

Rather than treating astrodynamics, engineering, and biology as isolated tasks, BeeYond Mars makes coupled spacecraft trade-offs (mass vs. delta-v, solar power drop-off near Mars vs. thermal regulation, telemetry throughput vs. power budgets) tangible without requiring prior aerospace expertise. In local 1–4 player pass-and-play mode, each role manages specific subsystems under one shared budget, teaching students and players how cross-disciplinary teams must communicate, share data, and iterate after failure—while connecting closed-loop off-world agriculture to the vital role of pollinators on Earth.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered:

Our creative approach blends an accessible retro 8-bit pixel-art narrative with rigorous astrodynamic and biological constraints, culminating in an explainable scientific paper rather than a simple "game over" screen. Key factors considered include real 2030–2031 Earth–Mars transfer windows, mass-to-delta-v penalties (0.008 km/s per kg), inverse-square solar irradiance drop-off, 4–24 minute one-way communication latency, planetary protection via sealed Martian domes, terrestrial Bombus terrestris diapause thresholds, and strict scientific honesty that distinguishes verified NASA/literature values from educational game abstractions.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used:

Built with zero external runtime dependencies using vanilla HTML5, CSS3, ES2022 JavaScript modules, HTML5 Canvas 2D (nearest-neighbor pixel rendering), Web Audio API (procedural 8-bit chiptune synthesizer), and Node.js (built-in test runner and static server), alongside Google Fonts (Pixelify Sans, Press Start 2P) and a custom Python-built bitmap font (aurelia-pixel.ttf). Trajectory mechanics were built and validated using NASA Ames Trajectory Browser, NASA General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT), and peer-reviewed entomological literature.
